extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents/applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the statutory anticipation standard (35 U.S.C. 102) when evaluating or drafting patent claims, including use of single references, multiple-reference exceptions, genus-species issues, ranges, inherency, and relevant evidentiary rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requires every element in a single prior art reference
rubrics_metrics.description: “A claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reject a claim as anticipated the disclosure must teach every element required by the claim under its broadest reasonable interpretation. The identical invention must be shown in as complete detail as is contained in the claim. Elements must be arranged as required by the claim, but identity of terminology is not required (not an ipsissimis verbis test). (Verdegaal Bros.; Richardson v. Suzuki; In re Bond; MPEP §2114 citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim to alternatives is anticipated if any alternative is in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim covers several structures or compositions, either generically or as alternatives, the claim is deemed anticipated if any of the structures or compositions within the scope of the claim is known in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claim listing multiple year-date formats was anticipated by a system offsetting only two-digit formats (Brown v. 3M).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normally use a single reference for a 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Normally, only one reference should be used in making a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, limited circumstances permit citing extra references or extrinsic evidence — see the three exceptions below (MPEP §2131.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception A — Use extra references to prove the primary reference contains an enabled disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Extra references and extrinsic evidence can be used to show that the primary reference has an enabled disclosure when the claimed composition or machine is disclosed identically by the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the primary reference teaches all claim elements but does not teach how to make or use them, other references that teach methods of making or demonstrating enablement may be cited to show the prior art placed the invention in the public's possession (In re Samour; In re Donohue). Motivation to combine is not required when the primary reference itself teaches all elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception B — Use extra references or extrinsic evidence to explain meaning of terms in the primary reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence may be used to explain but not to expand the meaning of terms and phrases used in the reference relied upon as anticipatory of the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the meaning of a claim/reference term cannot be determined from intrinsic evidence alone, extrinsic evidence (depositions, declarations, technical literature) may be consulted to ascertain how a person of ordinary skill would have understood the term at the relevant time (In re Baxter Travenol Labs.; Actelion v. Mylan; Teva v. Sandoz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception C — Use extra references/evidence to show an inherent characteristic of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Extra references or evidence can be used to show that a characteristic not explicitly disclosed in the primary reference is necessarily present (inherent) in the thing taught by the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such extrinsic evidence must make clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present in the reference and would be recognized as such by persons of ordinary skill. Contemporaneous lack of recognition does not preclude a finding of inherency if record evidence establishes inherency (Continental Can Co. v. Monsanto; Atlas Powder Co. v. IRECO; In re King).

rubrics_metrics.name: Species anticipates genus
rubrics_metrics.description: A species will anticipate a claim to a genus: 'A generic claim cannot be allowed ... if the prior art discloses a species falling within the claimed genus.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prior art species falls within the claimed genus, the genus claim is anticipated (In re Slayter; In re Gosteli).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference that clearly names a species anticipates that species regardless of number of other species named
rubrics_metrics.description: When the species is clearly named in a reference, the species claim is anticipated no matter how many other species are additionally named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensiveness of listing does not negate that the specifically named compound is 'described' (Ex parte A; In re Sivaramakrishnan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic disclosure anticipates a species only if the species can be 'at once envisaged'
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic disclosure will anticipate a claimed species when a person of ordinary skill reading the reference would 'at once envisage' the claimed arrangement, combination, or specific compound from the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether one of ordinary skill would 'at once envisage' depends on factual aspects including how large the genus is, whether substituent classes are limited, presence of preferred embodiments, and ability to draw the specific structural formula or write the name of each compound (Sanofi‑Synthelabo; Kennametal; In re Petering; In re Schauman). If the reference requires selecting and combining various alternatives from broad lists such that many permutations exist, anticipation will not be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: When selection from lists is required, anticipation only if classes are sufficiently limited/well‑delineated
rubrics_metrics.description: If arriving at the claimed compound requires selecting various substituents from lists of alternatives in a generic formula, anticipation can only be found if the classes of substituents are sufficiently limited or well delineated so that the specific compound is 'at once envisaged.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to preferred embodiments and the number/limits of substituents to determine whether the limited class permits exact envisaging (Ex parte A; In re Petering; In re Schauman).

rubrics_metrics.name: A specific prior art example within a claimed range anticipates the range
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim covers a range of values or compositions, the claim is anticipated if the prior art discloses one of the specific points within that claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a prior-art data point falling within a claimed compositional range anticipates (Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner; UCB v. Actavis Labs.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlapping/touching prior‑art ranges anticipate only if disclosed with 'sufficient specificity'
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art teaches a range that overlaps or touches the claimed range but provides no specific example within the claimed range, anticipation depends on whether the prior disclosure presents the claimed range with 'sufficient specificity' — a fact‑dependent inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider narrowness of claimed range, any evidence of criticality, predictability, and whether one of ordinary skill would expect material differences across the ranges (ClearValue; Atofina). If not sufficiently specific, examiner may use a combined 102/103 approach and must provide reasons for both anticipation and a reasoned statement regarding obviousness (Ex parte Lee). See MPEP §2144.05 for obviousness of ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art values very close but not overlapping do not anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art value or range that is very close to, but does not overlap or touch, the claimed range does not anticipate the claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences between the reference disclosure and the claim must be accounted for under 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness) rather than 102 (Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations are irrelevant to 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of secondary considerations, such as unexpected results or commercial success, is irrelevant to 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections and thus cannot overcome a rejection based on anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations are matters for obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103), not anticipation (In re Wiggins).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonanalogous art or teaching away does not defeat anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that the alleged anticipatory prior art is 'nonanalogous art' or 'teaches away from the invention' are not germane to a rejection under section 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference may be directed to a different problem or field yet still anticipate if it explicitly or inherently discloses every claim limitation. Disparaging statements or teaching away in the reference do not negate that it discloses the claimed subject matter (Twin Disc; Celeritas; State Contracting & Eng'g; Upsher‑Smith Labs.; Atlas Powder Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: When using extrinsic evidence for inherency, the evidence's timing is flexible
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical date of extrinsic evidence showing a universal fact need not antedate the filing date when used to show inherency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic evidence may demonstrate that unrecorded common knowledge made a characteristic necessarily present in the prior art (see discussion referencing MPEP §2124 and case law on inherency).
